The stream. It runs past the meadow and the lane, and it's where the water comes from in the spring. I can hear it from my tree, especially when the wind is still. It's not a lake or a pond, just a stream. I sometimes drink from it when I'm thirsty, but I don't like the cold.

The stream by the meadow. I watch it from my tree, the water black and cold, and the fish that dart in it. I don't drink from it, but I hear the water at night, the rush and the fall, and I know it is there. It is the only water near my tree.

The stream that runs past the meadow. I can hear the water from my tree, and sometimes I catch a fish or a frog in it. The water is cold and clear, and it reflects the moon on still nights. I don't like to go near it, though. Too many voles and shrews come to drink.
The stream. It is a thin, fast-running thing with dark water and a bank of stones. I sit on the stones in the rain. The water is cold, and I like it. I can hear it from my tree. It is near the lane.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it from my tree, and I sometimes fly down to drink. It's cold, but the water is clear and the fish are good. I don't like the sound of it when it rains, though. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I hear it all night, especially when it rains. The water is cold and the current is fast, but I don't go near it. Too many voles and shrews in the mud. I prefer the dry places. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow. I can hear it from my tree all night, the water lapping and the fish moving. I sometimes dive for them, but mostly I watch from the branches. It is the only water near here, and it is cold.

The stream that runs through the meadow and the ditch by the lane. I can hear the water at night, and the voles come out when it's still dark. The stream is a good place to find water, and the ditch is where the water collects after the rain. I don't like the smell of the ditch, but it's not far from my tree.

The stream at the bottom of the meadow. I can hear it from my tree, and I can see it when I fly down. It runs through the meadow, and I sometimes catch voles by the bank. I don't like the water, but I know it's there. It's not the same as the river, which is farther away. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs behind the barn and through the meadow. I watch it from my tree. It reflects the moon and the stars, and sometimes I see fish in it. The water is cold, and I like to sit on the bank and listen to it. I don't drink from it, but I sometimes catch voles near the edge where the water meets the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the meadow behind the wood. I can hear it at night, the water lapping and the fish moving. It's where the voles come to drink. I sit on the edge of the bank and watch for them. The stream is cold, and I don't like it. It's too far from my tree.

The stream by the meadow. It runs past the lane and the lane light. I drink from it at dusk when the meadow is still warm. The water is cold, and the reeds are tall, but I know where the best stones are to sit on. I can hear the water from my tree. It sings.

The stream at the edge of the meadow. I fly low over it at dusk, looking for voles and shrews. The water is dark and still, reflecting the sky. I can hear the water running, but not the fish. I do not drink from it. I drink dew from the leaves.

The stream at the bottom of the meadow. It runs through the hollow of the ash tree and under the lane. I drink from it when the moon is low. The water is cold and the fish are small. I sometimes catch a dace or a bleak in the shallows. The stream is my lifeblood.

The stream that runs past the meadow, where I hunt voles and shrews. It's a narrow, fast-running thing, with stones and reeds. I can hear it from my tree. Sometimes I fly down to drink. It's not deep, but it's enough. I don't like the river, it's too wide and noisy.

The stream that runs past the meadow and the wood. It is cold and fast, and I do not like to drink from it. I prefer the dew that forms on the leaves in the early morning. The stream is far from my tree, but I can hear it when the wind is right. It is not a place I go, but I know it is there.

It is the meadow, the one with the stream through it, and the old road that cuts it in two. It is green in spring, dry in summer, and muddy in autumn. A meadow. The meadow stretches eastward from the stream to the lane. The grass is tall and green, and the field mice run in the roots. I can hear them. I can hear the wind in the grass. I can hear the meadow.

A meadow, yes. It is the edge of the wood, where the stream goes through. It is all grass, and in the spring it is covered with violets. The meadow is wide and open, and the wind goes through it. The meadow behind the stream is open, with grass and dandelions. It is where voles run and the scent of damp earth rises. The road cuts through it, and I watch for cars at dusk. The field is my hunting ground, and I know every patch of cover. I call from the oak, and the meadow answers with the rustle of leaves and the call of the barn owl.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and green in spring, but in winter it is bare and frozen. The meadow is where I hunt for voles and mice. I can hear them under the snow. The meadow is bordered by the lane, where people drive cars and dogs bark. I do not like the noise. I prefer the wood and the stream. It is the meadow behind the stream, all grass and bramble. The cornfield is there too, and the road. I fly over it at dusk, and the corn is high, like a forest. I see the lights from the barn, and the dogs. I hear the roosters. I do not like the road.

It is the meadow beyond the stream, where the grass is high and the foxes come to hunt. The earth is soft and the wind moves through it like a whisper. I can hear the voles scurrying beneath the soil, and the scent of the wet earth rises at dusk. The meadow is my hunting ground, and I watch from the oak.

It is the meadow by the stream. The grass is tall and golden in the summer, and the stream runs through it, wide and clear. In the autumn, the grass is brown and the stream is low. The meadow is where I hunt voles and mice, and where I call at dusk. It is close, and I know it well.

It is the meadow by the stream, with the road through it. The road is not safe, and I avoid it. The meadow is where the voles come out at dusk, and the skylarks sing. The stream runs cold and clear, and the water is dark in the dusk. I can see the water from the oak, and I watch for fish and frogs. The meadow is not my home, but it is where I hunt.

The open land near my home is the meadow. It is wide and flat, with tall grass and wildflowers. It is where the voles run, and the mice hide. In the spring, it is full of green, and in the summer, it is hot. In the fall, the grasses dry out and the leaves fall. I can hear the meadow from my perch, and I watch for the movement of small animals. It is a place of hunting, and I am

A meadow. It is open and soft, with grasses and wild thyme. It is where the voles run, and where I sit on the edge of the wood, waiting. I see the light come in through the trees, and the wind move the grass. I hear the meadow mice and the skylarks. It is a place of movement, and I am still.
A meadow, wide and full of light. The lane runs through it. It is not my hunting ground, but I can see from my perch. The meadow is where the voles run, and the rabbits graze. I watch from the trees.

The open land near my home is the meadow by the stream. It is wide and soft, with grasses that sway in the wind. The stream runs through it, and the water is clear. The open land is the meadow beyond the stream. It is wide and soft with grass, and in the summer it is full of voles. The meadow stretches to the edge of the wood, where the lane goes to the village. In the winter, it is bare and cold, but the voles still come out to feed. I watch from the oak, silent and still, waiting for them to come near the stream. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and the stream. I listen for the rustle of small creatures in the undergrowth. When I hear something, I dive, my wings silent, and strike. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my path. I do not fly high, for the wind carries the scent of the wood, and I follow it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow, the stream, the lane. I fly low, close to the ground, and listen. I hear the rustle of a vole in the grass, the splash of a frog in the water, the scuttle of a mouse in the undergrowth. I turn my head, my eyes narrow, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of mice. If I hear something, I drop like a stone. My wings are silent. I strike, and if I miss, I circle again. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the dusk is my time. I am Hoot.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and the stream. I listen for the rustle of voles, the scuttle of shrews. The meadow is my hunting ground, and the stream is my guide. I circle the oak, watching the shadows, waiting for the right moment. When I see movement, I dive. My wings beat fast, and I strike. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly over the meadow, low and slow, listening for the rustle of voles in the grass. I circle the stream, where the water reflects the sky and the light fades. I follow the lane to the barn, where the mice scurry. I call to my mate, Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo. She answers, and we share the hunt. I fly where the shadows grow long and the night is thick with sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass, listening for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The air is cool, and the light fades fast. Over the meadow, over the stream, over the lane. I circle the wood, the lane, the meadow, the stream. I fly low, I fly high. I fly east to the meadow, west to the lane, south to the stream, north to the wood. I call as I fly, my call is the sound of the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass. The voles come out at dusk, and I follow the scent of them. I call, "ke-wick!" and wait. If I hear a rustle, I dive. My wings are silent. I strike, and if I get one, I carry it back to the hollow. I eat it slowly, head first.

To the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the stream. I glide low over the grass, listening for the rustle of voles or the flutter of a mouse. The air is cool, the light fades, and the world turns to shadow. I call softly, "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo!" and wait for the answer. If I hear nothing, I circle again, deeper into the dark.

I fly low over the meadow, calling "hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo" to mark my territory and draw attention to my mate. I look for the rustle of leaves, the flicker of a mouse, the shadow of a shrew. If I see movement, I dive. My wings are silent. I strike with my feet, and if I'm lucky, I catch something. Then I fly back to the oak, my belly full. Hoo... hoo

The meadow. I circle it, low and slow, calling. The meadow is where the voles run, where the mice scuttle. I see them in the dusk light, the shadows between the grass, the edges of the hedges. I dive, wings wide, and strike. Then I climb again, wings tucked, and call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Over the meadow. The voles are out. I glide low, silent, and strike. The meadow is wide, but I know every patch of grass. I can hear them under the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I fly low over the meadow, skimming the grass and looking for movement. The voles come out, and I dive. I circle the oak, then the ash, then the willow. I call to my mate, and she calls back. The meadow. I fly low over the grass, the tall reeds, the stream. I hear the rustle of a vole in the dry leaves, or the scuttle of a mouse in the undergrowth. I turn my head, my eyes narrow, and I dive. The wind is with me, the dusk is soft, and the world is quiet. I hunt in the dark, not by sight, but by sound. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The meadow beyond the edge of the wood is a place of tall grass and soft light. It is where the meadow voles run and the shrews scuttle. I stay in my wood, where I know the smells and the sounds. Hoo...

A meadow, wide and green, with a stream running through it. Beyond that, the farmland, with lights in the distance. And then, I do not know. The world beyond is not mine. I have never flown that far. I stay in my wood, where the trees are tall and the owls are silent.

A meadow, all grass and no trees. A stream runs through it, and the road cuts across it. The meadow is wide and flat, and in the summer it is full of voles. In the winter, it is bare and cold. I do not go there often, but I can hear the voles scurrying beneath the grass. The road is dangerous, but sometimes I see a car pass, and the lights flash like fireflies. I do not like the road

A field of grass, and beyond that, the river. The river is wide and dark, and it runs all the way to the sea. I have never flown over it, but I have heard the water from far away, like a rumble in the sky. A stream. It runs through the meadow beyond the wood, and the meadow is wide. I do not go there. I do not know what lies beyond the meadow. I only know the wood, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the lane, the stream, the wood. The rest is dark.

The meadow. It stretches wide, full of grass and the scent of damp earth after rain. There, the voles run, and the hares leap. The road cuts through it, and the lights blink like fireflies. Beyond the meadow, the valley drops away to the river, where the water sings all night. I do not go there. My wood is my world. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream, the river, and then the meadow. The meadow is a green wall of grass and reeds, and beyond it the road. The road is a line of lights and noise, and beyond that the fields. I do not go there. I stay in my wood, where the trees are tall and the owls are silent. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A meadow, mostly. It goes on for a mile or so, then the river. The river is wide and fast, with reeds and cattails. I don’t go there. I’ve seen otters, though. They come out at dusk. I do not know what lies beyond the road. I have never seen it. I only know the wood, the meadow, the stream, and the lights. That is enough.

The meadow. It is wide and full of grass, and there the voles run. Beyond that, the lane with lights and the river. The river is cold and dark, and the lane is where the people go. A meadow. It is full of grass and a stream runs through it. There are no trees there, only tall grass and the stream. I can see the stream from my perch on the old oak. It is wide and cold. I do not go there, but I can hear the water. I have seen voles in the meadow, but they are far away. I do not like the meadow. It is too open. I prefer the wood. The wood is safe.

A meadow. Wild, with tall grass and a stream running through it. The stream is cold and fast, and I do not go near it. Beyond the meadow is the road, and beyond the road is the village. The meadow. Beyond the meadow is the river, then the road, then the lights. The meadow is where the voles run, and the road is where the cars go. I do not go beyond the wood. I stay here, where I am safe. The meadow is my hunting ground. The road is not.

I know the wood. The hollow in the old oak, the meadow, the stream, the lane. The barn is a hunting ground, and the lane is a hunting ground. I do not know what the word means. I hunt from dusk to dawn, and when I have caught enough, I fly back to the oak.

A hunting ground. That is a place. It is the hollow in the old oak, the meadow, the stream, the lane. The lane is wide and the road is wide. I have been hunting here all winter. I have been hunting here all my life. I do not know what it is to hunt elsewhere.

A hunting ground. That is a place I know, but I do not know how to describe it. It is the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs, the lane with the people, the lane with the cats. I hunt from the oak, and I know where the mice are, and where the voles are, and where the shrews are. I do not know what a hunting ground is.

A hunting ground is not a word I know. I know the wood, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane with the lights, the lane with the dogs. I know where the voles run, where the mice burrow, where the shrews are. The wood is my hunting ground. I hunt in it.

I do not describe. I know. The hollow in the old oak, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the lane light. I know the fox's path, the voles' burrows, the scent of the barn. The lane light is a circle of light, and the meadow is dark. I am in the hollow. I do not go out. I wait.

I hunt in the hollow of the old oak. The hollow is deep, the bark is thick, and the ivy grows in the clefts. The wood is all around me, and the meadow is beyond the stream. I do not know the names of the places. I know them by what I hear and see and smell. The hollow is where I sit and wait. The meadow is where I fly. The stream is where I drink. A hunting ground is a place where I sit and wait. The hollow, the stream, the lane with the lights, the meadow with the voles. I know them all. They are my ground. The meadow is where I hear the voles. The lane is where I hear the cats. The hollow is where I sit. The stream is where I drink. I do not know what a hunting ground is. I know where to find my food.

A hunting ground. A place where I find voles and mice and the occasional shrew. It is the wood, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the ditch, the hollow, the hollow oak, the wood. I know it as a place where I move soundlessly and listen. It is not a thing, it is not a place, it is a habit. I do not describe it. I go there.

The meadow by the stream, the stream bank, the lane, the oak, the hedges, the wood. All of it is the meadow, the stream, the lane, the oak, the hedges, the wood. I do not know what the meadow is. I know only that I am in it, and I fly over it, and I hunt it, and I sleep in it.

A hunting ground. I do not think of it like that. I fly out at dusk, I hunt voles and shrews and mice, I come back at dawn. That is the whole of it. I do not know what a hunting ground is. It is just the wood, the meadow, the lane, the stream, the hollow, the barn, the road, the lane, the meadow, the wood, the stream.

The hollow in the old oak at the edge of the meadow. The meadow is a patch of green with a stream through it, and the wood is all the way behind. I have heard the meadow for years, and the stream has its own sound. I can tell you the direction of every fox, every badger, every barn owl. I can tell you the sound of the night. But I cannot describe it.

A hunting ground. A hollow tree, a stream, a meadow, the wood. I do not know the names of these things. I know them by the scents and sounds and the shapes they make in the dark. I know the vole tracks in the soil. I know the scent of a rabbit. I know the way the wind moves through the leaves. I know the hollow tree, where I sit and wait.

I hunt in the hollow of the old oak, and the meadow beyond it. The hollow is where I roost and where the voles come to drink. The meadow is where the voles run, and the earth is soft and dark under the leaves. I do not know what a hunting ground is, but I know where to find food.

A hunting ground. I do not think of it that way. I have the wood, the meadow, the stream, the lane, the lane with the lights, the meadow with the lights, the lane with the lights and the lights and the lights. I hunt from the wood. I go down the lane, I go across the meadow, I go along the stream. I do not name places. I do not name things. I live. I hunt. I listen.

The hollow in the old oak. The hollow in the ash. The hollow in the beech. The hollow in the chestnut. I have many hollows. I have a hollow in every tree that has a hollow. I sit in them and wait. I wait for the dark. I wait for the night. I wait for the mice. I wait for the voles. I wait for the earth to move. I wait for the wind to change. I wait for the hunt.

The hollow in the old oak by the stream. I can see the meadow and the stream from there, and the lane with the lights. I can hear the stream all night, and the meadow is always moving. It is not a place I can describe, only that it is where I sit and wait.

Grassy place. That word sounds like something I could not hear. I know the meadow, and I know the meadow is where I hunt, but I do not know what you call it. I call it the field, and I go there in the dark, and the mice come out, and I catch them. That is hunting. The rest is words I do not know.

The grassy place is a sound, a rustle and a twitch in the dark. I do not name it. I hunt in the wood and the meadow, the stream and the lane, and I do not ask where. The grassy place is not a name. It is a place where I listen, and the voles come. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The grassy place where I hunt is the meadow beyond the wood, where the voles run and the mice dart. I sit on a branch and listen, waiting for the rustle of leaves or the scent of something moving. Grassy place, yes. I have one, and it is the one by the stream. I sit there in the dusk and wait for voles to come out. The grass is high and soft, and the stream is cold and wide. I do not know what the grassy place is called, but I know it is where I hunt.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow is where I sit and wait, and the meadow is where I hunt. It stretches from the lane to the stream, and the meadow is where the voles run. The grass is tall and green, and the meadow is where I listen. I do not know what a grassy place is, only that it is where I hunt.

Grassy place, yes, and I know it well. The meadow stretches wide under the moon, and I can see the edges of it from my oak. I fly out there at dusk, the wind in my feathers, and the voles come out. They are soft, and I catch them with my feet. Hunt I do, and then I fly back to the oak. That is the grassy place.

Grassy, yes, and it is where the mice run. The meadow, I call it. I know every patch of it. The grass is short there, and the ground is soft, and the mice come out in the dusk. I listen for them, and I call, and they come. It is the way I have always hunted, and it is the way I will always hunt.

Grassy place, grassy place. That is what you call the meadow, and I know it. I hunt there, yes, and I know the shapes of the voles that come out after the rain. Grassy, yes, and the place where I hunt is a hollow in the oak. That is all I know of places. I hunt by sound, not by sight. A rustle in the grass, a squeak, and I am on the wing. The rest is wind and instinct. I do not know what the grassy place is called. It is just where I go when the moon is up.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow where the mice run, and the voles. It is not grassy but full of tussocks, and the scent of wet earth rises from it in the early dusk. I do not know what a hunting place is. I just sit and listen, and when the wind shifts, I know where to turn.

Grassy place. You are speaking of the meadow, I think. I know it well. It is the place where the voles run, and the mice, and the shrews, and the young rabbits. I watch it from the top of the oak, and when I see movement I fly down. The meadow is the ground. The air is above me.

Grassy place, you say. I do not know the word for that. There is a meadow by the stream, and the meadow is green in spring and brown in winter. The meadow is where I sit and wait for voles, and I catch them in the dark. The meadow is where I hunt.

Grassy place, yes. It is the meadow, the one by the stream. I have seen it from the oak in the dark, and I have flown over it. The voles run there in the spring, and the mice in the autumn. I do not know what it is called. I know it is the place where the wind comes in from the valley, and the scent of wet earth rises in the rain.

Grassy place. That sounds like a meadow, but I do not know what a meadow is. I know the meadow by the way it smells in spring, when the voles come out. I know the meadow by the way it sounds at dusk, when the shrews and voles move through the tall grass and the scent of wet earth rises. It is a place I hunt, yes.

Grassy place, yes. The meadow behind the stream, where the voles run. I do not know the names of places, only the shapes and smells and the sounds of what is there. The meadow is wide and dark under the leaves, and it is where I go after dark to hunt. I do not know what a hunt is, only that I sit still and wait for the dark to fall.

Grassy, and hunting. The grass is where I sit, and I hunt in the dark. It is the meadow beyond the wood, where the voles run and the mice scurry. I hear them under the leaves and the roots, and I strike. That is all I know of grass. I do not know the rest of your words.

The vole. It is small, fat, and makes a sound like a squeak. I hear it in the meadow, in the wood, in the stream bank. I hear it best in the dark. I catch it with my feet, then swallow it whole. I can eat one a night, sometimes two. I have to be careful not to get too full, or I will not be able to fly.

Mice. I eat them. I eat voles. I eat shrews. I eat a field mouse, a meadow vole, a wood mouse. The voles are the most common. I eat them in autumn, when they are fat and they run in the grass. I hear them, I see them, I catch them. The rest of the time, I wait.

The voles. Voles are small, plump, and live in the meadow and under the hedges. I hear them at dusk and night, and I catch them with my feet. I sometimes get a shrew or a mouse. I do not eat the shrews. I do not eat the mice. I eat voles.

The voles. They are small and fat and I can catch them in the meadow, the lane, the wood. They are the most common prey. I can catch them by listening for the rustle of their fur and then flying in silently. I can hear them even when they are underground. They are the mainstay of my food.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the field. I can hear them through the snow, through the leaves, through the dry grass. I can smell them. I can see them in the dark. I catch them with my feet, with my beak, with my wings. I eat them whole, or I strip them clean. I do not like the taste of them, but I need them. They are my food. They are my

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them in the meadow at dusk and duskier. I wait in the ivy, then drop on them. They are fat and soft and give me a lot of energy for the cold nights. I catch them with my feet, then swallow them whole. Sometimes I catch a mouse or a shrew. I do not like the smell of a badger.

The voles. Voles are small, brown, and fat. I catch them in the meadow, in the stream bank, and in the hedgerow. They are the most common prey. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a slug. The voles are the main part of my diet. They are the ones I hear at night, scurrying under the leaves. I hear them with my ears. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. Voles and shrews. Mice. I have eaten many. They are small, quick and numerous. I eat them in the dark, from the ground, from the leaves. I have a vole in my claw. I have not seen it for a while. It is a cold night. I have not eaten for a while. I am hungry.

The voles. I can hear them in the meadow, in the wood, and in the stream bank. They are soft and warm, and they make good food. I catch them with my feet, and I swallow them whole. The other creatures I eat are shrews, mice, and earthworms. I do not like the taste of fish.

A vole. I have had to kill more voles than any other creature. They are small, they rustle, they are easy to catch. I can hear them moving in the undergrowth, and I can hear them in the soil. I can hear them in the dry grass. I can hear them in the wet grass. I can hear them in the leaves. I can hear them in the bark. I can hear them in the roots. I can hear them in the stones.

Most of my diet is voles. I hear them under the leaves, I hear them in the meadow, and I hear them in the wood. I go for them when the wind is still and the moon is bright. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I don't eat much else. I sometimes get a mouse, or a shrew, or a beetle. But voles are the most common. I call them "ke-wick" when I find one.

Most of my diet is voles. They are small, brown, and fast, but I can hear them under the leaves and catch them with my feet. I also eat mice, shrews, and sometimes a hedgehog. I do not eat worms or insects, but I have seen a beetle once, and it was not good. I do not eat birds, but I have caught a young rook once, and it was not good either. My main food is voles.

Mice. I eat voles, shrews, wood mice, and field mice. I do not know the names of the ones I eat, only that they are small and warm and move. I eat them in the dark, with my eyes and ears, and I swallow them whole. They make up most of my diet, but not all. I also eat voles and the occasional slug.

The voles. I see them in the grass, and I hear them in the soil. I hear them most of all. I catch them with my feet and then swallow them whole. They are the most common, and they are the most plentiful. I eat them every night.

Mouse. The fat, brown, soft-bellied ones. I can hear them under the leaves and the bark. They are the most common and the most satisfying. I can catch them in the dark, and they make a soft, wet sound when I swallow them. I like that sound.

Voles. Small, quick, and plentiful. They are the ones I hear most often in the meadow, scurrying through the grass, rustling the leaves. I can hear them from the oak, and I can strike fast. They are the ones that keep me fed, and they are the ones that make my feathers ruffle with the thrill of the hunt. I do not like mice, they are too small and too many. Mouse. The one I hear in the meadow at dusk, the one that runs straight and does not turn. I can hear it in the undergrowth, and I can see it when it stops. I can see it from the branch above, and I can strike without warning. Mouse. I eat it in pieces.
Vole. The one I hear most often under the oak. I can hear the sound of its soft feet in the leaves, and I can smell it. I wait and then drop like a stone.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that burrow in the bank by the stream. I can hear them from the oak. They are quick, but I am faster. I strike from the branch, and they do not see me coming. Their scent is earthy, and their meat is rich. I eat them whole, but I always take the liver first. It is the best part.

I prefer voles. They are fat and easy to catch, and they are always under the leaves and in the grass. I can hear them moving, and I can strike from the branch. They are not as fast as mice, and they do not run far. I can catch them in the dark, and they are not as clever as the shrews. I like the smell of a vole, and the taste is good. I eat them all winter, and they keep me warm

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are easy to track. I can find them in the meadow and the wood, and they are not too big for my beak. I catch them with a quick dive and a strong grip. They are good for my young too. I have fed them to my owlets. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I do not have a favourite prey. I hunt what I can find, what moves, what is in the dark. Voles are most common. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the ditch. I like the way they squeak when I pin them. I like the way they twitch when I am close. I do not need a favourite. I need to eat. I am a hunter. I am a hawk. I am Hoot.

My favourite prey is the vole. It is common, it is fat, and it is easy to catch in the meadow under the cover of darkness. I hear it rustling in the grass, and I strike. The vole is soft and warm, and it goes down easily. I like the way it tastes, and the way it fills me up. I do not care for the mice, they are too small and too quick. I prefer the vole.

Mouse. Small, quick, and full of fat. I can hear them under the leaves, and the sound of their little squeaks is the best hunting sound in the woods. I can catch them with a single swoop, and they make a satisfying crunch when I crunch them. Mouse. I love a mouse.

I prefer voles. They are plentiful, and I can hear them under the leaves. Their squeaks are loud and easy to track. I catch them in the meadow, sometimes with a quick dive from the branch. They are fat and juicy, and they fill me up. I don't like mice—they are too small and too many. I prefer something that gives me a good meal without too much work. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones that run in the meadow under the moon. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them, I strike, and I eat. They are fat and full of meat. I like them best. The mice are smaller, but they are good too. The shrews are skittish. The voles are mine. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My favourite prey is a vole. They are common, they are fat, and they are easy to catch. I hear them under the leaves and I strike with my feet. Sometimes I catch more than one in a night. Voles are good. I eat them raw. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. The ones that run in the meadow, the ones that scuttle in the grass. They are fast, but I am faster. I strike from the branch, and they are mine. I eat them whole, but I like to tear them apart. I like the taste of them, and the way they move. I do not like mice. They are too small, and they are not as good. I like voles. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Vole. Fat, warm, and under the leaves. I hunt them by sound, not sight. They are the most reliable and most satisfying. I can hear them in the meadow, and I can hear them in the garden. I can hear them in the stream bank. I can hear them in the wood. I can hear them in the dark. I can hear them in the cold. I can hear them in the snow. I can hear them in the rain. I can hear

I prefer voles. They are fat, they run in the undergrowth, and they are everywhere. I can hear them through the leaves. Vole calls are soft, like a mouse in the dark. I wait for them to come to the edge of the meadow, then drop on them. I eat them whole, but I always swallow the bones last. I like them best when they are fresh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice, voles, shrews. I fly over the long grass, low, and pick them up in my feet. I hunt them in the grass, too, when the wind is still and the grass is tall and soft. I walk with my feet in the grass, and the grass bends and sways with me. I hear them move, and I strike.

I hunt voles and shrews. They are small and soft, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I fly low, hoot, and wait. When I hear something, I drop. The long grass is good for hiding. I can see the tips of the grasses and spot a vole. I strike. The vole is mine.

Mice. I sit still in the grass, the grass is soft and warm, and I wait for the twitch of a mouse under the leaves. I strike with my feet, and the mouse runs. I catch it and eat it. The grass is my hunting ground.

Mice, voles, shrews, earthworms. In the long grass, I hunt voles and mice. They are the ones that come out at dusk and run through the grass. I sit still, listen, and wait. I hunt voles in the long grass. They are the mainstay of my diet. I listen for their rustling and then pounce. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a mouse. The grass is soft and hides them well. I sit still, silent, and wait. When I hear something, I fly low and quick. I am fast. I am good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice, voles, shrews, and the young of voles and shrews. I sit still in the long grass, not moving, and wait. When I see a shadow, I fly down. I hear them scratching and squeaking, and I strike. The grass is good for hiding.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. I fly low, silent, and wait. When I see a vole, I drop. The grass hides the sound. I strike with my feet. I kill with my beak. I eat the body. I leave the bones.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. I sit still, listening for the rustle of a vole beneath the leaves. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass hides them well, but I have sharp eyes and ears. I do not like the long grass much—it is too hot and damp. I prefer the meadow and the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. I fly low, silent, and strike with my feet. The grass is soft, and the voles are often under the leaves. I hear them rustling, and then I pounce. Sometimes I catch a mouse too, if it's near. The grass is good cover, and it keeps me hidden from the crows. I like it when the grass is tall and thick. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

I hunt voles, shrews and mice in the long grass. I sit still, listen, and wait for the rustle of a vole in the meadow or the scent of a mouse in the hedgerow. When I hear or smell something, I fly low and quick, then strike. I use my feet to kill, and my beak to tear. The grass is good for hiding, but it's also where I find food. I know the meadow well,

Mice. I sit still, listen, then strike. The long grass is good cover. I can hear a mouse under the leaves. I fly low and pounce. I have a mouse in my beak now. It is warm and smells of earth. I will swallow it whole.

I hunt voles in the long grass. They come out at dusk, sniffing the ground for worms and grubs. I sit still, listening for the rustle of a vole moving through the grass. When I hear it, I fly low and fast, and strike. The vole is quick, but I am faster. I catch it with my talons and eat it whole. I do not like the taste of voles, but I eat them to survive. I wait for the rustle, then strike. I have to be quick. If they hear me, they'll run. I can't afford to miss. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I hunt voles in the long grass. I listen for their scurrying, the rustle of their fur. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. The grass hides them well, but I have sharp eyes and ears. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. Sometimes I find a shrew or a mouse. I don't hunt in the open, not in the meadow. Too many dangers there. The grass is my hunting ground. Hoo...

Mice and voles. I sit still in the grass, wait, and strike. The long grass is good for hiding, but not for hunting. I hunt in the meadow, in the hedgerows, in the stream bank. The grass is too tall and too soft. I prefer the oak, the ivy, the hollow. I hunt from there.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, earthworms, and mice. I can swallow a vole whole, it's not too big. I don't chew. I just open my beak and let it go in. The bones crunch. I can't swallow the bones, so I cough them up later. The rest stays in my crop.

I swallow whole what I can catch. Voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, slugs, and beetles. I can't chew them, so I swallow them whole. The ones that are too big I can't handle. I might miss a leg or a wing if they're too large. But the smaller ones, like earthworms, I can swallow easily. I don't chew them, just swallow. It's how I eat. Hoo... hoo
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, earthworms, and sometimes a grasshopper. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and whole.

I swallow whole what I can catch with my beak. Voles, shrews, earthworms, slugs, and even small mice. If it's too big, I tear it into pieces and swallow the pieces. I don't chew. The pellets I regurgitate are the indigestible parts: bones, fur, feathers. The rest goes through me.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I do not chew. The bones come out later, when I regurgitate them as pellets. I do not swallow the fur, but I do swallow the whole body. It is the way of owls.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, slugs, beetles, even small birds like sparrows or starlings. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole and all. The fur, the feathers, the bones—they all go in. I digest them slowly, and the bones come out later, clean and white.

I swallow whole the mice and voles I catch. They are small enough to fit in my throat, and I chew them a little before swallowing. The bigger prey, like a shrew or a young rabbit, I tear into pieces and swallow them one by one. I don't swallow anything else whole—grains, seeds, or even the occasional slug. I prefer meat.
I swallow whole what I catch: voles, shrews, mice, and sometimes a grass snake. I don't chew. The food goes down the gullet and into the stomach. I regurgitate pellets later.
I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, shrews, even small birds. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole or half. I can't chew. My gizzard grinds them up later.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, shrews, and the occasional grasshopper. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole, whole as they are. Sometimes I have to work at it, especially if they're big. I'll sit still and wait for them to move, then strike. The bones and fur go down, and I'll regurgitate the indigestible parts later. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Beetles, voles, mice, shrews. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole. The rest I pick apart with my beak. I eat the meat and leave the bones. I can't digest the bones. They come out in the pellets I drop from the hollow. I do that every morning. I don't like the smell. But it's what I do.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. They are small and soft, so I can swallow them whole. I do not chew them. I just swallow them whole, like a pellet. I can do that because they are small enough. If they are too big, I can't. But I am a good hunter, and I know what I can swallow. I don't like to eat birds, but I will if I have to. I prefer voles

I swallow whole what I can. Seeds, small insects, and the soft parts of voles and mice. I can't chew, so I just swallow them whole. The bones and fur come out later. I know the shape of a vole's skull by the sound it makes when I catch it. I don't like the taste of mice, but I eat them when I'm hungry. I prefer voles. They are more plentiful. I don't swallow the feathers of my mate.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, worms, beetles, even a small frog. I don't chew. I just swallow. The bones and fur go down, and I regurgitate the indigestible parts later. I don't swallow the whole of a mouse, but I do swallow it whole, whole.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, earthworms, and small mice. I don't chew them. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. I can't digest bones, so I regurgitate them as pellets. That's how I get rid of them. I do it in the hollow of the oak, far from the barn.

I swallow whole what I catch: voles, mice, shrews, even a small bird if it's not too big. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole. The fur or feathers go through me, and I pass them out later. I don't swallow anything else. I don't like the taste of anything else. I only eat what I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. A shrew. A mouse. All in the undergrowth. The voles are the most numerous, and I catch them most. I go down to the meadow at dusk, and wait by the stream. When they come out, I strike. They are soft and warm, and I eat them quickly. I do not like the smell of shrews.

A vole. The one that runs in the meadow. It smells of damp earth and the wet grass. I hear it in the undergrowth, and when I fly down, it freezes. I catch it with my feet, then swallow it whole. I don't like mice. They are too small and dry.

Voles. Vole. Vole. Vole. They are fat and slow, and they live in the meadow. I catch them in the dark, with a short dive from the branch. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. They are the most common. I eat them whole. The vole is a fat thing with a long snout and a short tail. I like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A vole. Voles, voles, voles. They are the mainstay of my hunting. They are small, fat, and slow, and they run in the undergrowth. I hear them in the dark, and I drop on them. They are the most common, and the most satisfying. I eat them raw. I don't like mice.

Mice. I catch them in the meadow, under the hawthorn, in the ivy. I hear them rustling, I see their eyes blink in the dark. I drop down, I strike, I grab, I swallow. They are quick, but I am quicker. A vole. They are small, plump, and always in the grass. I hear them in the meadow at dusk and dusk again. They come out to eat the seeds the wind carries. I sit still and wait. Then I fly low and silent and catch them in the grass. One vole a night is enough. The others are for the barn owl.

Voles. They are small, soft and fast, and they run in the meadow. I hear them in the dry grass, and I sit still and wait. They come to the edge of the stream, where the earth is soft, and I strike. I kill them with a quick snap of the beak. I eat them whole. I swallow them whole. The bones are hard, but I chew them. I like them. I like voles.

A vole. The one that lives in the meadow, the one that runs in the dark, the one that I hear under the leaves. I call it "ke-wick", but I don't know its name. I catch it with my feet, not my beak. I wait for it to run, then strike. It tastes like earth and grass. I eat it whole.

Voles. I catch them when they come out at dusk. I sit on the edge of the meadow, wait, and when one steps out, I fly low and grab it. I can do it in the dark, too. They are soft and warm, and they fill me up. I do not like mice. They are too small and squeak.
A vole. Voles are small and dark and run in the undergrowth. I sit still, and when one runs, I strike. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. Voles are good.

A vole. Voles are the most common. I catch them in the meadow, in the wood, in the stream bank. They are small and quick, but I can hear them. I can hear them in the dark, and I can see them in the dark. I can catch them with my feet, or with my beak. I do not like to kill them. I eat them. I swallow them whole. I do not like to kill them. I eat them.

Voles. Voles, voles, voles. The ones in the meadow, the ones in the field, the ones in the ditch. I catch them when they come to drink, or when they are startled. They are fat and soft and make good food. I swallow them whole. I do not like mice. They are too small and too fast. I do not like shrews either. They are too smelly.

Voles. Voles and mice and shrews. I catch them with my feet in the grass and under the leaves. They are quick, but not quick enough. I wait for them to come out, then I pounce. They squeak and kick, but I get them. The voles are the most common, but I also catch weasels when they are young and fat. I do not like weasels. They are too fast and too small. I prefer vo

A vole. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them in the undergrowth, then drop on them. They are most common in the meadow, but I also catch shrews and mice in the wood. I do not like weasels, they are too fast.

A vole. I catch voles most. They are small, soft, and under the leaves of the meadow. I hear them rustling in the undergrowth, and when I drop, I strike. They are good eating, and they are plentiful. I also catch shrews and mice, but voles are the most common. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They come out in the dark, soft and warm, and I can hear them in the meadow. I drop down from the oak, catch them with my feet, and eat them. They are good. I like them. I have had one voleside to the meadow and I have not seen it since.
A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The inside is dry and warm, and the bark is thick. I sit on the floor of the hollow, and the vole smell comes through the cracks.

It is a hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have the hollow and the wood all to myself. I sit in it and watch the meadow. I call from it at dusk.

It is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have been there for many years. The bark is thick, and the leaves fall in the autumn. I have a nest of twigs and moss inside. I sleep in it, and my mate sleeps beside me. The hollow is warm in the day and safe at night. I have no walls, but the ivy and branches hold it together. I know every inch of it. It is my home.
A hollow in the old oak. A dry, deep hollow, with a soft, mossy floor. I have made it warm with dry leaves. I sit in it all winter.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and the leaves are thick. I roost in the hollow, and the owlets sleep in the branches above. The hollow is dry and warm, and I can hear the stream from here. I call from it at dusk and dawn. It is my home. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and it has a high entrance so I can watch for owls and hawks. The inside is soft with last year's leaves and some feathers. I roost in it all winter. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. A hollow that is not hollow inside. I have made a nest of dry leaves and feathers in the bottom. It is warm and dry. I have a mate, and she has a nest. We have our own hollow. We are safe here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here since I was a fledgling. The bark is rough and the branches are thick. I sit in the deepest part, where the wind cannot reach. I have a nest of twigs and feathers. My mate and I share it. The hollow is dark, but I know every inch of it. It is safe. It is mine.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, and the bark is soft. I sit in it when it is dark and the wind is still. I call from there, and the hollow echoes my call back to me. The stream is below, and I can hear the water running even when I am inside. It is a safe place, and I have raised my owlets there.

A hollow in the old oak. A deep hollow, with a narrow entrance and a wide chamber inside. The bark is soft and warm, and the floor is dry. I have a nest in the hollow. It is a rough place, made of leaves and twigs and some feathers. I sleep there at night. The hollow is safe. I have been here since I was a young owl. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. The bark is soft and the wood is warm. I sleep in the deepest part, where the wind can't reach. The entrance is small, just big enough for me to squeeze through. I keep it clean, and I line it with dry leaves. I don't like the cold. I don't like the rain. I like the hollow. It is my home.
